den0: 10-Second Balance Test: One-Leg Stance Timer and Age Averages | İhsan Eren
den1: Can you stand on one leg for 10 seconds? Try it with the timer, compare yourself with the average for your age, and learn four exercises to improve your balance.
den3: Can you stand on one leg for 10 seconds? In a study that followed 1,702 people aged 51–75 for about 7 years, one in five could not, and their death rate during follow-up was markedly higher. This simple test is not a diagnosis, but it is a valuable clue about your balance. Try it with the timer below and compare yourself with the average for your age.

den63: If I cannot stand for 10 seconds, is my risk of early death high?
den64: This is not a diagnosis. The study shows that the death rate in the following years was higher among those who could not do the test; but this is an association, and the test itself does not indicate any disease. The researchers note that they could not account for factors such as recent falls and physical activity. You can treat the test as a warning light, start working on your balance and, if you are concerned, talk to your doctor.
den66: In the study that produced the age averages, participants chose the leg themselves. If you like, you can try each leg separately and compare.
den67: Why is it so hard with the eyes closed?
den68: To keep our balance we combine information from the eyes, the inner ear and the sensors in the soles of the feet and the joints. Closing the eyes removes one of these. The averages show a big difference too: at ages 18–39, 44.7 seconds with eyes open and 15.2 seconds with eyes closed.
